Gauss's Law with Points, Spheres, and Concentric Spheres

Both Young & Freedman and Openstax show the details of Gauss's Law with points and spheres. Both books then ask questions at the end of the chapters regarding concentric spheres.

The figures below show spherically symmetric charge distributions and corresponding regions of space.

 

 

The figures below show some of the same geometries and the corresponding E vs. r graphs. 

 

 

For each region of space in the figures above, the left hand side of Gauss's Law transforms as follows:

∫E⋅da=∫Ecosθda=∫E(1)da=∫Eda=E∫da=EA=E(4πr2)∫E⋅da=∫Ecos⁡θda=∫E(1)da=∫Eda=E∫da=EA=E(4πr2) 

where r is the radius of the Gaussian surface. By symmetry, the vectors E and da are always parallel, so θ=0θ=0  and cosθ=1cosθ=1 . The magnitude of the electric field is the same at all points of the Gaussian surface, so it comes outside of the integral. Then  the integral of all the same surface areas is the total surface area of the Gaussian surface which is 4πr24πr2 .

The right hand side of Gauss's Law QinsideεoQinsideεo transforms depending on the expression for Qinside. For a uniform charge density, ρ=QinsideVinside=QtotalVtotalρ=QinsideVinside=QtotalVtotal  which means Qinside=QVinsideVQinside=QVinsideV
